articles.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.snippet: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.
articles.full_text:
No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
- Published
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
- Published27 October
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
articles.snippet: The US president's promotion of Miller, a loyal partisan firebrand to be his new chief of staff sets up likely clashes with Congress.
articles.full_text:
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
- Published
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.
One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.
He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.
He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.
He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.
Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.
The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
Trump names Stephen Miller as new White House chief of staff
- Published20 hours ago
'Trump's psyche': The aide driving president's most controversial policies
- Published9 February
Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats â and some Republicans.
"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.
Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.
On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-President JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.
Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.
"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.
At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

Paraguay's president impeached and under house arrest after bank collapse
- Published
Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
PeÃ±a was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
articles.snippet: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
articles.full_text:
Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
- Published
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

articles.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
articles.snippet: Pope Leo travels to Uruguay just three weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.
articles.full_text:
Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.
The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.
The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.
"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.
"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.
In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".
He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.
He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.
Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.
On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.
The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

articles.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
articles.snippet: The 82-year-old appeared in court in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented.
articles.full_text:
Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
- Published
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.
At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.
Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.
He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.
The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.
In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

articles.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
articles.snippet: There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
articles.full_text:
Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
- Published
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.
The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.
Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."
"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.
Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.
Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.
Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.
He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , external
Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.
The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.
Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.
Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.
The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

articles.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.snippet: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
articles.full_text:
AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
- Published
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
'Market purgatory'
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

Strong jobs figures could ease market fears
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers killed in armed attack
It happened in a region of the country known to have drug trafficking activity.
A Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers have been killed in an armed attack, according to the country’s authorities.
The attack on Friday targeted Congressman Julio Portillo, who was in the town of Rio Hondo, in the eastern Zacapa department, which is known for drug trafficking activity.

Portillo was initially taken to a hospital with serious injuries. His death was later confirmed by the National Unity of Hope party, or UNE, to which he belonged.
“President Luis Contreras, members of the Board of Directors and lawmakers mourn the tragic passing of Congressman Julio Cesar Portillo Paz, representative of the Zacapa district,” Guatemala’s Congress posted late Friday on X.
President Bernardo Arevalo said the three National Civil Police officers killed in the attack had died in the line of duty and instructed security forces to cooperate with prosecutors investigating the killings.

articles.title: European troops set to train in Poland for postwar Ukraine deployment
articles.snippet: Britain and France will lead 2,800 troops from 11 nations in a two-week exercise testing how to move, protect and supply a force to rebuild Ukraine’s military after the war ends.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Thousands of European troops will gather in Poland next week for the Coalition of the Willing’s first major military exercise, a rehearsal for deploying a multinational force to Ukraine once the war with Russia comes to an end, European officials announced this week.
The exercise comes as U.S., Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are set to meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11, special envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday. The meeting caps a tumultuous year for Ukraine’s peace talks, which stalled after the U.S. and Israel began striking Iran in February and revived only in September, when Witkoff and fellow envoy Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv for their first visit as negotiators.
Britain and France will jointly lead KOALICJA 26.2 from Nov. 9 to 22, bringing together 2,800 troops from 11 nations for coordinated activities in Poland, France and Turkey under the coalition’s military arm, the Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U). American troops will not participate.
The drills will combine air, land and sea forces to “test how to move, protect and supply a force that would help rebuild Ukraine’s Armed Forces once the fighting ends,” according to a British Ministry of Defence statement.
Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Turkey and Britain are also taking part.
The training will prepare troops for the force’s eventual missions, which could include securing critical infrastructure, training Ukraine’s military, helping protect the skies and clearing mines from the Black Sea, as part of a broader package of security guarantees for Ukraine, according to the French ministry’s statement.
“This exercise shows the UK is stepping up, alongside France and our allies, to prepare for the day peace comes to Ukraine. This isn’t a hypothetical plan; it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops,” British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in the ministry’s release.
The MNF-U will reportedly not have a peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring mandate or operate under NATO command. It would move into Ukraine only after a ceasefire and at Kyiv’s request.
Ceasefire monitoring “would be a different task from that of the multinational force, whose aim is different in nature because it is meant to support the Ukrainian army in its ability to be beefed up,” former French Ambassador to Ukraine Gaël Veyssière told Military Times in April.
The drills will also test “command-and-control arrangements for the force” and assess “how different components can integrate and operate effectively as one multinational force,” according to the British release.
Britain is sending 300 personnel, including soldiers from the British Army’s 7th Light Mechanised Brigade, known as the “Desert Rats,” to rehearse logistical movements. Warsaw will manage the movement of MNF-U troops after the war but will not send its own soldiers into Ukraine. Nearly 2,000 Polish soldiers will take part in addition to the foreign forces, the Polish ministry said.
France is sending “hundreds” of troops, including a unit equipped with about 50 “contact drones,” the second of its kind after one deployed to Romania, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Jacques de Montgros’s told lawmakers last month.
Turkey will not send troops to Poland, the French ministry said, but will stand up the MNF-U’s maritime element in Istanbul, “testing arrangements for maritime mine clearance to allow commercial shipping to safely return to Ukraine’s ports,” according to the British release.
“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said the commander of MNF-U, British Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman.
The exercise announcements do not specify the final size of a force that could deploy to Ukraine, but Britain and France said earlier this year that they were prepared to contribute roughly 5,000 troops each.
Even a minimal “tripwire” presence would require 10,000 to 25,000 troops, the Center for Strategic and International Studies assessed last year. Because only a third of any force is frontline-ready at a given time, rotations push that number far higher, Ed Arnold, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former British military officer, told Military Times.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected allowing a foreign troop presence in Ukraine, and he warned in September 2025 that Western forces deployed there would be legitimate targets.
Although the MNF-U is not a peacekeeping force, Polish defense officials said its presence is meant to ease Ukrainian fears of a renewed Russian attack once the war ends.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pressed allies on Wednesday to move quickly, pointing out that Russian forces continue to batter Ukraine’s power grid and other critical infrastructure as the country braces for its fifth winter of full-scale war.
“Peace has no alternative, and postwar security guarantees must be truly cast-iron,” he said.

articles.title: US Army feeds culinary soldiers new job title
articles.snippet: Formerly known as culinary specialists, a soldier with the 92G occupation identifier will henceforth be known as a “tactical field feeding specialist.”
articles.full_text:
Army cooks have a new name — and it’s a real mouthful.
Formerly known as culinary specialists, a soldier with the 92G occupation identifier will henceforth be known as a “tactical field feeding specialist,” the service announced this week.
The Army unveiled the new title during a late-October ceremony at Fort Lee, Virginia, and the service said the change comes as it shifts to training for large-scale combat operations, meaning soldiers who prepare meals also need to understand battlefield logistics in a contested environment.
Stars and Stripes first reported the shift.
“When we change an MOS title in the Army, we do it not for superficial rebranding or administrative convenience; we do it because the character of war has changed,” Col. Stacy Moore-Callaway, Quartermaster commandant, said in a recent release. “We formally redesignate our culinary specialists, stepping forward under the title that truly captures the 92G’s operational weight, and that is to turn them into tactical field feeding specialists.”
The Army formalized the position of cooks — then known as 94B Food Service Specialist — in the 1960s, and in 1995, the specialty was redesignated as 92G Culinary Specialist.
Cooks use Army Field Feeding Systems and Mobile Kitchen Trailers, and cooks are responsible for managing ingredient ordering, inventory and food preparation.
“Our tactical field feeding warfighters deliver endurance to the force,” Sgt. Maj. Paul Denson, Installation Operations Directorate, Army G-4, said during the ceremony.
“I submit to you that a well-fed warfighter is a lethal, agile, and adapted soldier that will win in a prolonged close fight,” he said. “We’re not simply producing food; we’re sustaining warfighters; a tactical field feeding specialist has to understand food production, nutrition, and food safety.”

articles.title: US, Colombian troops kick off exercise amid the Pentagon’s Western Hemisphere pivot
articles.snippet: Hundreds of American and Colombian troops kicked off a sprawling military exercise in Colombia this week as the U.S. military sharpens its focus on the Western Hemisphere.
articles.full_text:
Hundreds of American and Colombian troops kicked off a sprawling military exercise in Colombia this week, training to navigate dense jungles and counter explosive threats as the U.S. military sharpens its focus on the Western Hemisphere.
Dubbed Exercise Southern Vanguard 2027, the exercise is the 41st iteration of the annual training event, which runs through mid-November, the Army announced this week. Hosted by the Colombian Army and led by the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, the drills involve roughly 350 U.S. military personnel and more than 400 Colombian soldiers.
After the event’s opening ceremony, the U.S. Army said joint exercises will focus on jungle warfare and counter-IED skills, with command post training, maritime interdiction, cyber skills and ground security.
The Colombian National Army’s Chief of the Force Generation Staff Brig. Gen. Edilberto Cortés extended a welcome to all of the exercise’s international participants.
“This presence demonstrates the shared commitment of our nations to strengthen collective readiness and consolidate the ties of cooperation that support our strategic and historical relationship,” he said in the Army’s release.
The exercise — which kicked off on Monday — is scheduled to run until mid-November, and troops planned to conduct medical evacuation drills from Colombia’s Tolemaida military base to its Cavalry School in Bogotá, according to a separate release.
In an extensive force restructure, the Army launched a the new Western Hemisphere Command in late 2025. The change reflects a broader shift in Pentagon priorities alongside the 2026 National Defense Strategy, which prioritizes defending the “U.S. Homeland” and Western Hemisphere over countering China.
At an annual U.S. Army conference in October, the service’s top commander for the Western Hemisphere characetrized American “economic supremacy” as a major goal of Washington’s regional security plans.
“The end state is economic supremacy for the United States,” Gen. Joseph Ryan, the commander of the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said during a panel discussion. Later, he added, “we have ceded control of that economic terrain in this hemisphere to the People’s Republic of China over at least the last two decades, and that is a major threat to our national security.”
The Pentagon has increasingly prioritized jungle warfare skills, launching a reinvigorated jungle school in Panama with the Panamanian armed forces and sending troops across the world to learn about and develop jungle warfare doctrine. In September, a U.S. official told Military Times that Colombian soldiers were soon coming through the reestablished “Green Hell” course.
The U.S. and Colombia have a long history of cooperation, and the U.S. has previously partnered with the country’s Lancero course, which is similar to Ranger School. Colombia also recently participated in PANAMAZ, a multinational exercise where forces simulated defending the Panama Canal.
Both countries are part of the Counter Cartel Coalition, chaired by the U.S.
Months before Exercise Southern Vanguard 2027, U.S. soldiers took part in Exercise Southern Vanguard 2026, which included another field training scenario in Sauce, Peru. It brought together roughly 400 soldiers for jungle training.

articles.title: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.snippet: Russia is already using its new Rassvet satellite network — billed as a homegrown version of Starlink — for military communications over Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence.
articles.full_text:
Russia is already using its new Rassvet satellite network — billed as a homegrown version of Starlink — for military communications over Ukraine, aiming to make its strike drones more accurate and harder to jam, Ukrainian military intelligence told Reuters.
Russia has launched 32 Rassvet satellites into orbit so far this year in two batches in March and July, according to the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense (GUR). The Russian government said last month that Russia had launched more than 30 satellites.
That is a tiny fraction of the more than 10,000 satellites in the Starlink network, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, the military version of which — Starshield — operates in Ukraine but not in Russia. Access to SpaceX systems, which Moscow does not have, has greatly helped Kyiv in the war against invading Russian forces.
Moscow plans more Rassvet launches by the end of 2026 to expand the network’s geographic coverage, gradually bringing it closer to a full low-orbit satellite communications system, GUR said in a written statement.
“Russia is using the ‘Rassvet’ satellite system over the territory of Ukraine for military purposes,” GUR spokesman Andrii Yusov said in the statement.
“The constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory: communication is available intermittently when the satellites pass over the relevant areas.”
Russia’s defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia’s Scientific and Expert Council warned of the risks posed by Starlink on Friday and urged a quicker deployment of the Rassvet system.
RENEWED UNCERTAINTY OVER US SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE
Starshield has given Kyiv a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications.
Russian forces had been using grey-market Starlink terminals in Ukraine until Kyiv successfully lobbied SpaceX to disable them earlier this year, one of several factors that shifted battlefield momentum in Ukraine’s favor this year.
However, last month Ukrainian battlefield commanders unexpectedly saw speed limitations imposed on Starshield, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forcing the cancellation of some strike operations.
No explanation has been given for the temporary restrictions on Starshield, which came amid tensions with President Donald Trump’s administration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and have now been lifted.
While Russia’s territorial gains on the front line have ground to a virtual halt this year, it has doubled down on strikes against Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure and cities, using a new generation of jet-powered drones that are harder to intercept.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly raised concerns about Russia’s attempts to build its own version of SpaceX’s network. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week imposed sanctions on 10 companies involved in developing Rassvet, including Bureau 1440 — the coordinator of the state-backed project.
Bureau 1440 has said it plans to create a constellation of more than 900 satellites by 2035. The company did not immediately respond to Reuters’ questions about Rassvet.
BOOST TO SURVEILLANCE AND STRIKE DRONES
The GUR statement said that Rassvet may provide Russia with two-way data exchange with its unmanned aircraft over Ukraine, allowing surveillance drones to transmit data in real time and pilots to adjust the route of attack drones during flight, reducing dependence on a pre-programmed flight path.
That could allow drones to adjust to changes in target location, or evade air defenses.
“In the longer term, this could increase the effectiveness of strike and reconnaissance UAVs and make it more difficult for electronic warfare and electronic intelligence systems to intercept them,” Yusov said.
Mykola Zientsev, a Kyiv-based security expert, said there were some signs that Rassvet was already having an impact on precision strikes by Russian jet-powered drones.
“In practical terms, Russia already possesses at least two high-quality satellite communications windows every day, each lasting more than an hour,” he wrote in a recent report. “That is enough to have operational consequences.”
GUR has published a list of 49 companies from Russia and Belarus that it says are involved in the project.
Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of GUR, said in an interview with Ukrainian media in August that Russia was launching the Rassvet system much faster than originally planned and Ukraine was already discussing ways to counter it.
Ukraine said in August it had carried out a long-range missile attack against the Progress rocket and space center in Russia’s Samara region, which produces rockets used to launch Rassvet satellites.
Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Washington, has urged the U.S. to impose its own sanctions on Rassvet companies. He also told Reuters that Russia was developing the Starlink analogue using Chinese components.
The U.S. Treasury Department had no comment on Ukraine’s push for further sanctions.

articles.title: US European Command launches vigilance campaign as hybrid threats mount
articles.snippet: U.S. European Command is calling on U.S. troops, family members, and civilian employees to stay alert for suspicious behavior and to cover their digital tracks while moving around Europe.
articles.full_text:
U.S. European Command is calling on troops, family members, and civilian employees to watch for suspicious behavior on and off military installations and to cover their digital tracks while moving around Europe.
Branded “See Something, Do Something,” the initiative is meant “to foster a proactive mindset” toward security and force protection, the command said this week. The announcement comes amid heightened concern about drone incursions and other hybrid threats to U.S. and allied military forces around Europe.
The initiative emphasizes protecting U.S. personnel and their families “as a shared responsibility vital to sustaining long-term combat readiness alongside global partners.” It encourages members of U.S. military communities to stay alert while in crowded public areas, like transit hubs, and report any “unusual behavior or unattended items” to military police or local authorities.
Troops and their families are also “urged” to practice “rigorous digital discipline” by reviewing their social-media privacy settings, disabling geotagging on fitness apps and mobile devices, and avoiding posting information about their locations and travels online. The announcement also cites a recommendation from security experts to vary daily commuting routes, travel times, and off-base activities “to reduce predictability.”
U.S. personnel and their families “are our most precious asset, and their safety is our highest priority,” Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, commander of U.S. European Command, said in the announcement. “By embracing a proactive security mindset and enhancing collective vigilance, we build a stronger force protection environment that keeps us safe and ready.”
European Command did not identify a specific threat that prompted the campaign, but it comes amid increased concern about “hybrid warfare,” — malign activity below the threshold of war that often lacks a clear perpetrator — involving Russia and targeting U.S. forces and NATO allies.
Russian misinformation and intimidation directed against U.S. military personnel and their families using social media and hacking has been a longstanding concern. But since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, that hybrid activity has become more aggressive and disruptive. A number of undersea pipelines and cables have been affected by what Western officials believe to be sabotage; GPS jamming and spoofing are more frequent, and drone incursions around sensitive sites, like military bases and airports, have increased.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating a failed attack with explosive-laden drones at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, which is a key logistical hub for Western supplies to Ukraine. Later in September, a tip about suspicious vehicles near the airbase RAF Fairford led to the arrest of several men in relation to a suspected terrorist plot in which British officials say Iran may have been involved. The incident prompted the US to remove the B-1 bombers that were stationed at the base.
In October, after the discovery of a drone with a canister of explosives near another German airbase, the German military raised its Russian sabotage threat assessment to “substantial” — its second-highest level — and warned that the threat was no longer confined to facilities where Ukrainian troops were being trained and to major military installations. More than 30,000 U.S. military personnel are stationed in Germany.

articles.title: US Air Force eyes reviving WWII air bases in the Pacific
articles.snippet: The U.S. Air Force hopes to conduct more than 6,000 aircraft operations annually at airfields on three American islands in the northwest Pacific Ocean.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force hopes to conduct more than 6,000 aircraft operations annually at four airfields on three American islands in the northwest Pacific Ocean, including a major WWII-era airfield that is being refurbished, according to an announcement from the Department of the Air Force.
The department published a notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement that will assess “potential social, economic, and environmental effects” of training and operations at Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport. The islands are part of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, an unincorporated U.S. territory.
The proposed training and exercises will support the Air Force’s Agile Combat Operations concept, which emphasizes dispersal of forces across airfields and the ability to maneuver between them while sustaining operations under a range of conditions, with the goal of thwarting an adversary’s ability to shut down those operations by targeting a single base. ACE, as it’s known, has developed largely in response to the Chinese military’s growing reach and expanding missile arsenal.
The notice said the four airfields provide “a unique opportunity” to support ACE, with infrastructure that varies from “fully developed commercial airfields to expeditionary operating locations.” The three islands are within a few dozen nautical miles of each other, which would allow for training that reflects the complexity of distributed operations while reducing transit time between them. They are less than 100 nautical miles north of the major military bases on Guam, another U.S. territory, which would support the staging and deployment of forces for those exercises.
The three airfields “collectively provide a training environment that enables [the Air Force] to exercise distributed operations, test and employ tailorable force packages, strengthen sustainment and maneuver capabilities, and enhance operational resilience,” the notice reads.
The environmental impact statement will evaluate the potential effects of the proposed activities, which include small, medium and large trainings and exercises held several times a year for a few weeks at a time and consisting of up to 1,200 fixed-wing and 320 rotary-wing operations, like takeoffs and landings, annually at each airfield. It will also assess an alternative scenario with up to 1,400 fixed-wing and 384 rotary-wing operations per airfield annually and a “No Action Alternative.”
The trainings and exercises would be supported by up to 550,000 gallons of fuel at each airfield, up to 1,000 personnel per airfield, the temporary installation of expeditionary infrastructure, the handling of munitions like chaff and flares, as well as support services and pre-and post-training and exercise activities.
The proposed activity comes after several years of work to upgrade the airfields in question, especially the airfields on Tinian, which were built and heavily used during WWII. North Field was inactive after the war and was largely covered with vegetation when the rehabilitation effort began in late 2023. The Air Force also upgraded port and roadway infrastructure, fuel pipelines and airfield surfaces, and utilities to facilitate expanded operations on Tinian.
The airfield rehabilitation efforts have created some questions among Air Force leaders about resourcing and funding, particularly as the war with Iran has placed new demands on the force. Island residents also have misgivings about the projects. While some welcome the investment that the construction and military operations will bring, others have doubts that the increased activity will really benefit the islands’ populations and that the Pentagon will be transparent about its activity and responsive to local concerns.
The Department of the Air Force will hold public meetings this month on Saipan, Tinian and Rota to get feedback on the proposal, with written comments due by Nov. 29. The department plans to produce a draft environmental impact statement for public comment in fall 2027 and a final version in mid-2028.

articles.title: Denmark, Lithuania latest Baltic navies to buy ‘Blocker’ mines through Finnish scheme
articles.snippet: Denmark is the latest country to buy Finland’s “Blocker” naval mines, a day after Lithuania decided to go ahead with its own contract for the weapon.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Denmark is the latest country to buy Finland’s “Blocker” naval mines, a day after Lithuania decided to go ahead with its own contract for the weapon.
The forces of Finland, where the mines are made, and Estonia already operate the proximity sea mines. Estonia bought them in 2021.
The Danish acquisition will take place as part of a pentalateral joint procurement agreement that includes Finland and Lithuania, as well as Germany and Norway, who have not yet publicly announced a contract to buy the device.
Lithuania’s ministry of defense similarly said that its procurement of Blocker was taking place under the Naval Mines Cooperation, a procurement agreement that grew out of a program launched in 2024.
Aside from joint buying, the NMC agreement is meant to “strengthen cooperation on logistics, training, exercises and the lifespan of the systems,” the Danish ministry of defense said.
The Finnish military signed a contract with manufacturer Forcit Defence in June on behalf of the five countries participating in the NMC’s procurement scheme. The contract was worth “hundreds of millions of Euros,” the Finnish government said.
Ten countries signed the pact’s original declaration of intent: Belgium, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Finland and Estonia, all of which are members of NATO.
Germany may still announce a procurement decision this year, German industry publication Hartpunkt reported, citing “well-informed circles.”
“Selecting Finland as the lead nation of the naval mines cooperation project is a reflection of the Finnish Navy’s long-standing capability in naval mining,” the country’s military wrote in a statement.
Forcit Defence advertises the Blocker mine as having the explosive power equivalent to a ton of TNT. It detects ships using a range of sensors.
Naval mines have been front and center in the news this year, with Iran’s use of the technology to block the Strait of Hormuz and hold a large part of global energy supplies hostage in response to the U.S.-Israeli campaign against it.
The Baltic Sea has also become a key point of tension, particularly since 2022, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, the sea is now entirely surrounded by the alliance, except for Russia’s Kaliningrad and Leningrad Oblast coasts. This is a strategic headache for Russia, whose ships must pass through the narrow Danish straits and onward through the Kattegat and Skagerrak to reach the open ocean.
Russia has repeatedly warned that it will not accept being cut off from the Atlantic. “If we do not give them a firm rebuff, the British, French and even the Baltic states will soon become so emboldened that they will try to completely block our country’s access to the seas, at least in the Atlantic basin,” said Nikolai Patrushev, President Vladimir Putin’s aide and chairman of Russia’s Maritime Board, in a February interview with Russian newspaper Argumenty i Fakty and reproduced by the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation. “If this situation cannot be resolved peacefully, the Navy will break through and eliminate the blockade.”

articles.title: Medical services company settles with 4 states over 2023 hack of sensitive patient records
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The case, brought by AGs in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York and Michigan, targeted the medical transcription, coding and imaging subsidiaries of the Nevada-based Perry Johnson Companies.
articles.full_text:
Medical services company settles with 4 states over 2023 hack of sensitive patient records
State attorneys general on Friday announced a health care services company has agreed to pay $300,000 and make sweeping changes to its security practices following a March 2023 breach exposing the data of more than 13 million people nationwide.
The case, brought by AGs in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York and Michigan, targeted the medical transcription, coding and imaging subsidiaries of the Nevada-based Perry Johnson Companies.
If the firm fails to make the required cybersecurity reforms, it will be required to pay the four states an additional $9.7 million, according to a press release from the office of New York Attorney General Letitia James.
James’ office launched a probe that found hackers broke into Perry Johnson’s systems by using an employee’s credentials. The company did not use multi-factor authentication to verify users, according to James’s office.
In the months following the hack, the bad actor hoovered up passwords and obtained unencrypted files storing patients’ protected health data, the press release said. While the company’s software found and recorded the hacker’s movements, it was allegedly poorly configured and did not flag the activity for the information security team.
The data theft continued unabated for two months with the firm allegedly only learning of the breach when the hackers alerted it.
The stolen records allegedly contained names, dates of birth, home addresses, Social Security numbers, hospital account numbers, diagnoses, insurance information and clinical information from medical transcription files. The files included patients’ medication names as well as diagnostic and lab test results, according to the press release.
The firm did not respond to a request for comment.
The terms of the deal require Perry Johnson to create a comprehensive information security program and incident response standards; establish multi-factor authentication, encryption and password management systems; implement yearly risk assessment programs and establish a system to properly manage the collection, use, retention and disposal of the health data it receives.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Certificate authority DigiCert reports data breach involving business customer info
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: DigiCert explained that over the summer, an internal business system was "externally accessible when that was not intended," and someone had created an unauthorized account.
articles.full_text:
Certificate authority DigiCert reports data breach involving business customer info
Internet security firm DigiCert reported a data breach involving an internal business system that was left exposed and eventually accessed by someone outside of the company.
The Utah-based company did not respond to requests for comment but posted a lengthy post-mortem on Mozilla's Bugzilla platform explaining the situation.
DigiCert, which is a certificate authority and offers other corporate security services, said the incident began in February 2025 when an internal business system was moved out of a VPN-restricted network, making it accessible externally. Certificates typically help to verify the security of web servers.
“Beginning on 2026-06-21, DigiCert determined that the business system was externally accessible when that was not intended, and that an unassigned account had been created,” the company said, adding that the issue was fixed by July 2.
On October 19, DigiCert confirmed that the database was accessed starting on June 27 and that it was a “reportable event.” The accessed data included customer names, business email addresses, phone numbers as well as documents like driver’s licenses, passports or utility bills and other info.
The report does not say how many customers were impacted.
A spokesperson for the company declined to say whether the attackers have contacted DigiCert, telling Recorded Future News that they are “focused on providing our customers with information relevant to them about the incident.”
“To our knowledge, there is no evidence of misuse of the information involved. We have reported the incident to law enforcement and will continue to support the investigation as needed,” the spokesperson said.
The company noted that the threat actors who accessed the database could not issue certificates or take other actions. Their certificate authority services were not affected and customer login credentials were not taken.
The report notes that the incident was reportable due to rules issued by Mozilla, Google Chrome, Microsoft and Apple.
DigiCert said the incident was not detected earlier because the system migration “was treated as an infrastructure change rather than a security change which would have triggered more detailed review and sign off.”
“The business system had insufficient alerting for new account creation through the externally-accessible endpoint or request volume from its internal endpoints,” the company said.
The issue caused alarm on social media as several people shared breach notification emails they received from DigiCert. Multiple posts expressed concern about the ability of threat actors to tie personal documents like IDs and passports to specific certificates.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.4 million in crypto from nation-state hackers
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts.
articles.full_text:
FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.4 million in crypto from nation-state hackers
A senior FBI official pleaded guilty to stealing millions in cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by nation-state hackers and theft victims.
Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts.
Yaroch was an FBI Supervisory Special Agent who worked at FBI Headquarters within the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division — with his work focusing on an unnamed nation-state.
He used his seniority to access FBI systems that had the codes and passwords necessary to take cryptocurrency from at least two adversarial nations as well as 10 victims of crimes. In total, he conducted 100 transfers from 79 wallets starting in December 2024. The wallets were connected to 35 different FBI investigations.
Yaroch had hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit card debt, loans and car payments. He paid off several large loans. The Justice Department gained access to his ChatGPT conversations, which showed he planned to buy a vineyard in Portugal and retire.
Yaroch began to make legal arrangements in Portugal and bought plane tickets to the country for him, his wife and his child slated for September. But he ended up confessing to the theft to a DOJ employee in July.
Yaroch told the DOJ employee, who he knew from a previous job, that he was angry about an investigation of a suspect from an unnamed adversarial nation. Yaroch "became frustrated when he could not do more to disrupt this individual's use of cryptocurrency.”
"Yaroch decided to tell [the DOJ employee] about his actions because of the shame and he knew what he did was wrong. Yaroch said it was ‘eating him up inside’ and he wanted to ‘get it off his chest,’” prosecutors said.
Further investigation revealed Yaroch had stolen millions and was often indiscriminate in his theft.
The Justice Department said his thefts ranged from 81 cents to over $580,000 in another fraudulent transfer.
Prosecutors said Yaroch's misuse of the cryptocurrency credentials that he stole from FBI systems “compromised multiple FBI investigations related to both criminal groups and nation state adversaries.”
His actions also exposed the FBI's investigations to the targets who controlled the wallets, compromising their sources and methods.
Yaroch will be sentenced in March.

articles.title: CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S. is working on extraditing three suspects from Europe in a case involving more than $100 million in fraud from CEO impersonations.
articles.full_text:
CEO-spoofing scammers used AI to help steal more than $100 million, feds say
The Justice Department indicted three men for allegedly scamming companies out of more than $100 million with help from AI.
Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit are accused of pretending to be company CEOs or lawyers and contacting lower-level employees to trick them into sending large payments to bank accounts they controlled.
Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer and Sheetrit was detained in the U.K. in September. The Justice Department said on Thursday that extradition requests for all three men are pending.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the three used artificial intelligence “to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives into sending them and their co-conspirators approximately $129 million.”
Hazan, 54, and Sheetrit, 42, are from Israel while Soall, 41, is Spanish. All three are facing up to 104 years in prison on multiple charges of money laundering, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud and more.
The men allegedly stole nearly $5 million from a hospital in Missouri, $2.6 million from a Rhode Island bank, $2.9 million from a hospital in California, $11.5 million from a tech company in the U.K., $4.6 million from a finance company in Massachusetts and $5.2 million from a Florida pet food company.
According to prosecutors, the conspiracy ran from 2024 to 2026 and involved the three as well as other co-conspirators deploying artificial intelligence as a way to spoof the voices and images of real corporate executives.
Court documents said several incidents involved the three men contacting employees and telling them they needed help with a confidential financial transaction, mimicking the CEO’s voice or image on the call.
To further the scheme, they would tell the employee to speak with lawyers at a large international firm that were working on the transaction — using AI to then make themselves look and sound like those lawyers.
The money was wired to accounts across the U.S., Europe, the UAE and China before the scammers transferred it to cryptocurrency.
Prosecutors said Soall typically impersonated the lawyers and had a script he used to mimic the attorneys. Hazan was in charge of laundering the funds, boasting in one instance of laundering $400 million since 1994, according to court documents. The Justice Department noted that Hazan was previously convicted of bank fraud in 2008.
Senior FBI official James Barnacle said criminals continue to weaponize emerging technology like artificial intelligence.
“The alleged scheme orchestrated by Soall, Hazan, and Sheetrit demonstrates how the use of advanced technology can be exploited to commit large scale fraud,” he said.
The FBI urged other companies that may have been victims to come forward.
